decisions.sentence: The table was read through the `dietary` lens.
`glucose` was chosen as the outcome; it is measured on all `21,849` rows.
The analysis was declared for `inference`: associations are estimated with their uncertainty.

Column roles were set for `28` columns: energy `kcal`; exposures `sugar`, `protein`, `carb` and 4 more; covariates `age`, `gender`, `cycle_begin_year` and 9 more; identifier `SEQN`; flags `imputed_weight`, `imputed_height`, `imputed_bmi` and 3 more; excluded `triglycerides`; `cycle_begin_year`, `bp_sys` and 13 more were proposed below high confidence and wait for their own confirmation before any default reads them.

The 7 columns `bp_sys`, `bp_di` and 5 more, proposed as covariates at medium confidence, below high, for one reason ("A person's characteristic, usually adjusted for rather than studied."), were confirmed together as one group, after the evidence for their proposal was read.
`cycle_begin_year` was confirmed as a covariate, on its own, after the evidence for its reading was read.
`hdl` was confirmed as a covariate, on its own, after the evidence for its reading was read.
`imputed_weight` was confirmed as a flag, on its own, after the evidence for its reading was read.
`imputed_height` was confirmed as a flag, on its own, after the evidence for its reading was read.
`imputed_bmi` was confirmed as a flag, on its own, after the evidence for its reading was read.
`imputed_waist` was confirmed as a flag, on its own, after the evidence for its reading was read.
`imputed_bp_sys` was confirmed as a flag, on its own, after the evidence for its reading was read.
`imputed_bp_di` was confirmed as a flag, on its own, after the evidence for its reading was read.
`kcal` was recorded as a day's energy in kcal.
`501` rows with `kcal` outside `500`–`5000` or not recorded were excluded as implausible intake.

Rows missing any predictor were dropped (a complete-case analysis): `2,943` of `21,348` rows remain; complete cases give unbiased coefficients only if whether a value is missing does not depend on the outcome, given the predictors (Groenwold et al. 2012; White & Carlin 2010).
No rows were held out: every analyzed row estimates the coefficients, and no cross-validated score is reported under inference: the declared model is reported by its estimates.

The analysis estimates the total effect of more sugar in place of other carbohydrate (total carbohydrate and energy fixed) on `glucose` (a substitution), as a difference in the mean outcome per unit of `sugar`.
For the effect of `sugar`, by the disjunctive cause criterion: `age` and `gender` are confounders, adjusted for.
For the effect of `sugar`, by the disjunctive cause criterion: `protein`, `carb`, `fat_total`, `fat_sat` and 2 more are confounders, adjusted for.
For the effect of `sugar`, by the disjunctive cause criterion: `weight`, `height`, `bmi` and `waist` are of unknown timing, left out of the primary model and adjusted for in a declared secondary one.
For the effect of `sugar`, by the disjunctive cause criterion: `bp_sys`, `bp_di`, `hdl`, `meds_hbp` and `meds_chol` are mediators, left out.
For the effect of `sugar`, by the disjunctive cause criterion: `cycle_begin_year` is a confounder, adjusted for.
Energy was adjusted by the standard (multivariate) model: `kcal` enters the models beside `sugar`, so each nutrient's effect is at fixed total energy.
`age` was confirmed to hold amounts or counts, on its own, as the question showed it.

`sugar` entered the models as a straight line; `protein` entered the models as a straight line; `carb` entered the models as a straight line; `fat_total` entered the models as a straight line; `fat_sat` entered the models as a straight line; `fat_mon` entered the models as a straight line; `fat_poly` entered the models as a straight line; `age` entered the models as a straight line.
`cycle_begin_year` was confirmed to hold codes for categories, on its own, as the question showed it.
One model family was chosen: linear regression.
The primary analysis was set beside `1` sensitivity analysis, each the same model on its own rows: `Every row`, keeping every row.

artifact.methods: The estimate of `sugar` is reported across a declared sequence of models fit on all 21,348 analyzed rows: unadjusted; Model 2, the primary, adjusted for `kcal`, `protein`, `carb`, `fat_total`, `fat_sat`, `fat_mon`, `fat_poly` and 3 more; Model 3, further adjusted for `weight`, `height`, `bmi` and `waist`, possible mediators, so not a total effect. Only the exposure's estimates are shown as effects; every other coefficient is listed apart as an adjustment term, not an effect estimate (Westreich & Greenland 2013, Am J Epidemiol 177:292). Influence was checked by Cook's distance against the median of F(19, 21,329) (Cook 1977, Technometrics 19:15): 0 rows above it. Sensitivity to unmeasured confounding is reported by the Cinelli–Hazlett robustness value (each adjusted covariate a named benchmark; its form for the 95% interval, and the benchmarks' intervals, are not reported, as they assume classical standard errors and the intervals reported are HC3) and by the E-value for the estimate and for the confidence limit nearer the null, never as a pass or a fail.
artifact.withheld: No estimate is shown until Fit is pressed: pressing it locks the analysis plan, so the plan is declared before any estimate is seen.

robustness.interval_note: The robustness value for the 95% interval and the benchmarks' adjusted intervals rest on the classical least-squares standard error (0.00624), as sensemakr computes them; the interval reported uses HC3 standard errors, 0.00607, so they are not reported: they would describe an interval that is not the one shown.

sensitivity.reading: An unmeasured common cause would need a partial R² of 3.0% with both `sugar` and `glucose`, beyond the measured covariates, to bring the estimate to zero (Cinelli & Hazlett 2020, J R Stat Soc B 82:39); one as strong as `carb` would move it to 0.02414. The robustness value for the 95% interval and the benchmarks' adjusted intervals rest on the classical least-squares standard error (0.00624), as sensemakr computes them; the interval reported uses HC3 standard errors, 0.00607, so they are not reported: they would describe an interval that is not the one shown. E-value for the estimate: 1.03, and for the confidence limit nearer the null 1.02 (VanderWeele & Ding 2017, Ann Intern Med 167:268); an E-value is read against the common causes one can name, never as a pass or a fail.

artifact.methods: The estimate of `sugar` is reported across a declared sequence of models fit on all 21,348 analyzed rows: unadjusted; Model 2, the primary, adjusted for `kcal`, `protein`, `carb`, `fat_total`, `fat_sat`, `fat_mon`, `fat_poly` and 3 more; Model 3, further adjusted for `weight`, `height`, `bmi` and `waist`, possible mediators, so not a total effect. Only the exposure's estimates are shown as effects; every other coefficient is listed apart as an adjustment term, not an effect estimate (Westreich & Greenland 2013, Am J Epidemiol 177:292). Influence was checked by Cook's distance against the median of F(19, 21,329) (Cook 1977, Technometrics 19:15): 0 rows above it. Sensitivity to unmeasured confounding is reported by the Cinelli–Hazlett robustness value (each adjusted covariate a named benchmark; its form for the 95% interval, and the benchmarks' intervals, are not reported, as they assume classical standard errors and the intervals reported are HC3) and by the E-value for the estimate and for the confidence limit nearer the null, never as a pass or a fail.

decisions.sentence: The table was read through the `clinical` lens.
`event` was chosen as the outcome; it is measured on all `600` rows.
`1` of `event` was taken as the event and coded 1; `0` was coded 0.
`event` was modeled as a `time_to_event` task, overriding the detected `binary`.
`event` was analyzed as a time to event, each row followed until `followup_years`, at the event or when follow-up ended without it.
The analysis was declared for `inference`: associations are estimated with their uncertainty.

Column roles were set for `6` columns: exposure `x1`; covariates `x2`, `grp` and `activity`; identifier `pid`; time column `followup_years`; `x1`, `grp` and `activity` were proposed below high confidence and wait for their own confirmation before any default reads them.
`x1` was confirmed as an exposure, on its own, after the evidence for its reading was read.
`grp` was confirmed as a covariate, on its own, after the evidence for its reading was read.
`activity` was confirmed as a covariate, on its own, after the evidence for its reading was read.
No rows were excluded: every row with `event` measured stays in the analysis.
A complete-case analysis was applied: no row is missing any predictor, so all `600` rows remain.
No rows were held out: every analyzed row estimates the coefficients, and no cross-validated score is reported under inference: the declared model is reported by its estimates.
The analysis estimates the total effect of `x1` on `event`, as a conditional hazard ratio per unit of `x1`, given the adjustment set.
For the effect of `x1`, by the disjunctive cause criterion: `x2` and `grp` are confounders, adjusted for.

For the effect of `x1`, by the disjunctive cause criterion: `activity` is a cause of the outcome only, adjusted for. Under a conditional hazard ratio, adjusting for `activity`, a cause of the outcome only, changes the conditional estimand, not only its precision: the ratio is non-collapsible (Daniel, Zhang & Farewell 2021, Biom J 63:528).
`x1` entered the models as a straight line.
`activity` was confirmed to hold amounts or counts, on its own, as the question showed it.
One model family was chosen: Cox proportional hazards.
The analysis plan recorded above was declared in TurboTab before any estimate was displayed (SHA-256 `22867306dfc4`); every later change is marked as made after the estimates were seen.

missing.assumption: Complete cases give unbiased coefficients only if whether a value is missing does not depend on the outcome, given the predictors (Groenwold et al. 2012; White & Carlin 2010).

concerns: The hazard ratio for `x1` may change over follow-up (Grambsch–Therneau p = 2 × 10⁻¹⁹, against 0.01 shared over 1 column): it is then an average over follow-up, not one constant ratio.

diagnostics.method: Proportional hazards by Schoenfeld residuals: the score test of each term's product with a function of time (one minus the Kaplan–Meier estimate), as R's cox.zph computes it (Grambsch & Therneau 1994, Biometrika 81:515)
diagnostics.reading: The hazard ratio of what you study changes over follow-up (χ²(1) = 87.37, p = 9 × 10⁻²¹, below the customary 0.05): the reported ratio is an average over follow-up.

sensitivity.reading: E-value for the estimate: 2.28, and for the confidence limit nearer the null 2.05 (VanderWeele & Ding 2017, Ann Intern Med 167:268); an E-value is read against the common causes one can name, never as a pass or a fail.

artifact.methods: The estimate of `x1` is reported across a declared sequence of models fit on all 600 analyzed rows: unadjusted; Model 2, the primary, adjusted for `x2`, `grp` and `activity`. Only the exposure's estimates are shown as effects; every other coefficient is listed apart as an adjustment term, not an effect estimate (Westreich & Greenland 2013, Am J Epidemiol 177:292). Proportional hazards were checked by Schoenfeld residuals on the Kaplan–Meier time scale (global χ²(5) = 88.78, p = 1 × 10⁻¹⁷); the check failed for the exposure, and no response is recorded yet. Sensitivity to unmeasured confounding is reported by the E-value for the estimate and for the confidence limit nearer the null, never as a pass or a fail.
